headline: Konnichi is from Middle Chinese 今日, the goon reading, so likely the original borrowing.
Asanebō is 朝 (asa, “morning”) plus 寝坊 (nebō, “sleeping in, waking late; someone who sleeps in”).
Shitagi is 下 (shita, “under”) plus 着 (-gi, “clothing”).
Kaigishitsu is 会議 (kaigi, “meeting”) plus 室 (shitsu, “room”).
Kagaku is Chinese 化學 (huàxué, literally “change + study”), first cited in Japanese in an 1860 translation of a Dutch text.
Itsu is from Old Japanese, and its first syllable may be a root shared with 如何 (ikaga) and 何処 (izuko).
Hiji is from Old Japanese, first attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE, from Proto-Japonic *penti.
Kami's kanji 髪 is a shinjitai, simplified from 髮.
Subete was originally the -te form of an Old Japanese verb 統ぶ (subu), compare 統べる (suberu).
Ii is a shift from 良い (yoi), classical 良し (yoshi), by way of seven steps from yo₂si.
Kugi is first cited to the Man'yōshu of circa 759 CE, from Proto-Japonic *kunki.
Kamisama is 神 (kami, “deity, god”) plus 様 (-sama, honorific suffix).
Karakau is attested in The Tale of the Heike (c. 1330); the kara may be cognate with 絡む (karamu, “to become entangled”), and the kau may be 交う (kau, “to exchange; to mix”).
Kakuritsu was coined by Matsumiya Tetsuo in 1908 as a translation of English probability.
Kagiru has an uncertain origin: it looks related to 鍵 (kagi, “key”), but Japanese references do not make that connection.
Shiri is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *siri, and its ultimate derivation is unknown.
Tsuitachi began as tsuki tachi: 月 (“moon; month”) plus 立ち (“standing; starting, occurring”).
Shugi is from Classical Chinese 主義 (zhǔyì), attested in the Records of the Grand Historian.
Tachimachi is apparently a shift from 立ち待ち (tachimachi, “standing and waiting”), first cited in the Man'yōshū of 759.
Kaku, “to scratch”, is cognate with 書く (kaku, “to write”).
Namida is attested as namita in the Nihon Shoki, and later the Man'yōshū has the ta replaced by da.
Izure is いづ (izu, interrogative pronoun) plus れ (-re, nominalizing suffix for demonstratives).
Yagate contracts 止難 (yamigate): the verb 止む (yamu, “to stop”) plus 難て (gate, “difficult”).
Jū, “ten”, is from Middle Chinese 十 (MC dzyip), with a literary Hokkien cousin, si̍p.
Ima ni is 今 (ima, “now”) plus に (ni).
The old spelling of tabi, 単皮, means a single (単) hide (皮): originally a leather shoe.
Ku, “nine”, is from Early Middle Chinese 九, the goon reading, so likely the initial borrowing.
Hoteru is borrowed from English hotel, itself from French hôtel.
Iidasu is ii, the stem of 言う (iu), plus 出す (dasu).
“To go back” is likely 逆 (saka, “reverse”) plus 上る (noboru, “ascend, go up”).
Kyoku, “office”, is from Middle Chinese 局.
